text: Ivan Ilyichs life had been most simple and most ordinary, and for that very reason, as the rest of the story slowly and painfully reveals, it had also been most terrible. <break time="0.8s" /> The son of an official, he studied law, took up a modest post in the provinces, and quickly learned to do whatever was considered proper by the people of high rank around him. <break time="0.8s" /> Like a fly drawn toward the light, he was drawn toward those who stood above him, adopting their manners and their views without ever asking whether they were truly right. <break time="0.8s" /> He married Praskovya Fyodorovna, a pretty girl of good family, not so much because he loved her deeply as because the marriage was pleasant to him and was approved by the right people. <break time="0.8s" /> When his wife grew jealous and demanding during her first pregnancy, he did not try to understand her but withdrew, little by little, into his work, where everything was orderly and under his control. <break time="0.8s" /> In court, he learned to strip away everything human from a case, reducing living people to documents and forms, so that he could deal with them coolly while still appearing polite and fair. <break time="0.8s" /> Thus his years passed, lightly, pleasantly, and decently, filled with official duties, comfortable dinners, and evening games of cards, and it never occurred to him that anything essential might be missing.
